extracted.intended_audience: citizens, policymakers, and readers of the New York Packet debating the Constitution and the merits/dangers of confederate vs. federal systems
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the structural strengths and defects of confederacies (historical examples and principles) to judge their capacity for order, defense, and longevity; used to argue for a stronger federal union. Emphasizes practical outcomes (anarchy, tyranny, foreign intrusion) arising from institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of strength into particular depositories
rubrics_metrics.description: The CONCENTRATION of large portions of the strength of the community into particular DEPOSITORIES, whether at the disposal of individuals (feudal nobles) or of political bodies (separate governments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures whether power/resources are centralized in entities (individuals or subordinate political bodies). The text warns this concentration produces rivalship of power and potential oppression: such depositories can rival the national government and resist or counteract legitimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular confidence and goodwill of separate governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate governments will generally possess the confidence and good-will of the people, which enables them to oppose encroachments of the national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the degree of popular loyalty to local/regional authorities. High local legitimacy strengthens their ability to resist a central authority — potentially preventing necessary national action and enabling persistent rivalry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rivalry between federal and member governments
rubrics_metrics.description: A rivalship of power exists between separate governments and the national government; this rivalry is a key point of similitude with feudal baronies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether institutional design encourages competition rather than coordination. Persistent rivalry can lead to instability, internal conflict, or the subversion of national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and effectiveness of sanctions for federal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The total want of a SANCTION to [the Confederation's] laws is a palpable defect — federal laws must have an effective sanction to be obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks if federal decisions are backed by enforceable penalties or means of compliance. Absent effective sanctions, laws become powerless on the members and the union is prone to disregard, evasion, or collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether federal authority substitutes law for force
rubrics_metrics.description: A good system substitutes the mild and salutary coercion of the MAGISTRACY (law) for the destructive COERCION of the SWORD (force/violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates whether conflict resolution and compliance are achieved through legal institutions and processes rather than by armed coercion. Systems lacking legal coercive mechanisms tend toward violence and arbitrary force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and character of federal deputies/representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal powers administered by deputies appointed wholly by the cities/states and exercised over them in the same capacities tends to produce weakness and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers how representatives are chosen and whether they act independently of their appointing units. Deputies who are merely agents of sovereign members may be swayed by more powerful constituents, corruptible, or ineffective at exercising federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rules (unanimity vs. majority) and effect on action
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements of unanimity (as in the United Netherlands) or other rigid consent rules render federal decision-making impracticable and lead to delay or circumvention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses constitutional voting/decision rules: unanimity can paralyze collective action (contributions, treaties); frequent departures from the rule or usurpation of powers may follow, risking either paralysis or arbitrary central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared federal institutions (treasury, troops, coin, judicatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of common treasury, common troops, common coin, or common judicatory (as with the Swiss cantons) produces a union that is little more than loose association and is fragile in crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examines whether uniform financial, military, monetary, and judicial institutions exist to bind members. Lack of these common instruments undermines the union's capacity for defense, enforcement, and economic coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to foreign intrigue and intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Confederacies that are internally divided or weak invite foreign influence, intrigue, and intervention (examples: Greece, Germanic empire, Netherlands, Poland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures exposure to external powers exploiting internal divisions. Weak federations can be manipulated by foreign actors, used to foment discord, or subject to territorial encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency for powerful members to tyrannize weaker members
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, the more powerful members of a confederacy often tyrannize over the weaker, producing satellites and subordination rather than equal sovereign partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates balance of power among members. Large imbalances allow dominant states to control federal outcomes or coerce compliance, undermining the union’s legitimacy and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of internal faction, jealousy, and ambition causing dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual jealousies, fears, hatreds, and injuries among members (or between leading members) can escalate into civil wars or dissolution (Peloponnesian War, Achaean league fate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses social/political fault-lines and the institutional capacity to manage faction. Without mechanisms to moderate faction, temporary alliances and rivalries can produce catastrophic breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on non-institutional supports (oaths, superstition, personal influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When federal power rests on oaths, superstition, or individual influence (e.g., Amphictyonic council's reliance on superstition), the practical efficacy of powers is undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates whether the authority of federal organs rests on stable institutions or fragile social/religious practices and personalities. Reliance on the latter is brittle and prone to failure in changing circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of intermediary subdivisions (circles/districts) to execute federal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to divide a weak empire into circles/districts to execute laws often replicate the same deformities and either fail or execute with devastation (as in the German circles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers whether creating intermediate administrative units improves enforcement. If those units mirror the larger constitutional defects (local interests, defaulters), they will be ineffective or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of constitutional reform due to sovereignty's repellant quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The repellant quality incidental to the nature of sovereignty prevents reforms founded on proper consolidation; powerful members resist changes that would consolidate authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses the practicability of amending or strengthening the union. Sovereign pride and entrenched privileges make constructive reform difficult without external pressure or extraordinary concord.
